title: African social cohesion combines broad tolerance with steep trust gradients, restrictive immigration attitudes, and weak institutional fairness
source_unit: Afrobarometer Dispatch AD1227, Social cohesion in Africa: Bonds, belonging, and the common good
geography: 38 African countries; Afrobarometer Round 10 interviews conducted in 2024/2025

observations.period: 2024/2025 Round 10; social trust and social distance

trust_relatives.unit: percent saying they trust relatives somewhat or a lot

trust_neighbours.unit: percent saying they trust neighbours somewhat or a lot

trust_different_ethnicity.unit: percent saying they trust people of a different ethnicity somewhat or a lot

trust_different_religion.unit: percent saying they trust people of a different religion somewhat or a lot

social_distance_gradient.value: Interpersonal trust declines sharply as social distance increases

observations.method: Afrobarometer Round 10 public-opinion survey across 38 countries, with comparative descriptive analysis of interpersonal trust by relationship and social distance.
observations.uncertainty: The cross-sectional survey captures reported trust at one period and does not establish whether contact, institutions, conflict, inequality, or identity causes the trust gradient.
observations.subgroup: People connected through family, neighbourhood, ethnicity, religion, nationality, and political affiliation across diverse African national contexts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower trust across social distance may reflect realistic caution or limited contact rather than generalized social fragmentation; close-group solidarity can also support wider cooperation under the right institutions.

different_ethnicity_neighbour.unit: percent who would welcome or accept a neighbour of a different ethnicity

different_religion_neighbour.unit: percent who would welcome or accept a neighbour of a different religion

different_party_neighbour.unit: percent who would welcome or accept a neighbour of a different political party

different_nationality_neighbour.unit: percent who would welcome or accept a neighbour of a different nationality

tolerance_trust_split.value: Tolerance toward difference is substantially higher than interpersonal trust across social distance

observations.method: Afrobarometer descriptive comparison of social-tolerance attitudes and interpersonal trust measures.
observations.uncertainty: Stated willingness to accept neighbours is not the same as close relationship, institutional equality, material inclusion, or willingness to share political power.
observations.subgroup: Ethnic, religious, political, national, and other identity groups living alongside one another under varied histories of conflict, migration, and state capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: High tolerance can provide a latent social resource for cohesion even where trust is lower; survey responses may also reflect socially desirable answers.

observations.period: 2024/2025 Round 10; immigration and boundaries of inclusion

immigrant_economic_contribution_positive.unit: percent saying immigrants make a positive contribution to the economy

immigrant_economic_contribution_negative.unit: percent saying immigrants make a negative contribution to the economy

fewer_or_no_foreign_job_seekers.unit: percent favouring admitting fewer or no foreign job seekers

fewer_or_no_refugees.unit: percent favouring admitting fewer or no refugees

inclusion_boundary.value: Immigration is a sharp boundary where broad tolerance does not automatically translate into open inclusion

observations.method: Afrobarometer cross-country descriptive analysis of perceptions of immigrants and preferences for admission of foreign job seekers and refugees.
observations.uncertainty: Attitudes vary by country and context; the report does not identify whether economic conditions, security concerns, identity politics, labour competition, or information environments drive the immigration boundary.
observations.subgroup: Citizens, immigrants, refugees, foreign job seekers, host communities, labour markets, and states managing mobility and belonging.
observations.counterinterpretation: Restrictive admission preferences can coexist with everyday hospitality and local solidarity, and may express capacity concerns rather than categorical hostility toward migrants.

observations.period: 2024/2025 Round 10; identity, fairness, solidarity, and civic action

national_identity_priority.unit: percent valuing national identity at least as highly as ethnic identity

equal_attachment_national_ethnic.unit: percent saying they feel equally attached to national and ethnic identity

government_ethnic_unfairness.unit: percent saying government sometimes, often, or always treats their ethnic group unfairly

powerful_interests_influence_judges.unit: percent saying powerful interests often influence judges

unequal_law.unit: percent saying people are often treated unequally under the law

informal_vs_civic.value: 47% sought help from relatives to make ends meet, 33% from friends or neighbours, but only 15% joined others to raise an issue with government

observations.method: Afrobarometer descriptive analysis connecting identity, perceived fairness, informal assistance, and reported collective civic action.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are not a causal chain; assistance, identity, legal fairness, and civic action may vary by country, crisis, wealth, conflict, and institutional access.
observations.subgroup: Ethnic groups, national citizens, families, neighbourhoods, religious or community organizations, and people with different access to courts and government channels.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong family solidarity may be a foundation for collective action rather than its substitute; low reported civic action may reflect risk, limited channels, or different forms of political participation.

related_sources.claim: Afrobarometer survey network and public data resources.

boundary: This record adds a pan-African social-cohesion layer connecting trust distance, tolerance, immigration, identity, perceived institutional fairness, informal solidarity, and civic action. It is a cross-sectional public-opinion profile, not respondent-level ingestion, a causal model of cohesion, a continent-wide uniform estimate, or proof that tolerance becomes equal treatment or collective political action.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Afrobarometer AD1227 page reviewed for the 38-country, 50,961-interview frame, trust gradient, tolerance, immigration boundary, national/ethnic identity, institutional fairness, informal solidarity, and civic-action findings.
